title: The Foundling Bride of Jerusalem
sum: In the longest chapter of this part, the LORD tells Ezekiel to make Jerusalem know her abhorrent things by telling her own story. She was an unwanted baby of Canaanite stock, thrown out in a field to die (16:1–5). The LORD passed by, gave her life, raised her, and later spread his cloak over her and married her (16:6–14). She grew famous for her beauty, then used his gifts to make idols, sold herself to Egypt, Assyria and Chaldea, and killed the children she bore him (16:15–34).

Her lovers will now strip and judge her (16:35–43). Her sisters Samaria and Sodom look righteous beside her, yet the LORD promises to restore all three (16:44–58). The chapter ends with a covenant that Jerusalem did not earn and an atonement that leaves her without a word to say (16:59–63). The language is blunt, and the Plain neither softens it nor adds to it.
readings: Read as a retelling of Jerusalem's history

The story follows the city's real past: a Jebusite town before David (16:3), a royal city under David and Solomon (16:13–14), a partner of Egypt, Assyria and Babylon (16:26–29), and a place of child sacrifice under Ahaz and Manasseh (16:20–21; 2 Kings 16:3; 21:6). The woman is a city, and her 'lovers' are nations and their gods.
Read as a courtroom speech

The verb in 16:2 is the prosecutor's 'make known'. The exiles at Ezekiel's house believed Jerusalem could never fall (11:15; 12:22). The chapter takes away the ground they stood on: the city's election was a gift to an unwanted child, not a reward, and it can be taken back.
Read through the marriage of God and his people

Jewish tradition made Sinai a wedding (Mishnah Taanit 4:8). Christian readers drew on the same image for Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 19:7–8; 21:2), and on the chapter's last verses for grace given to the undeserving.

views.H: The chapter walks through Jerusalem's history: the Jebusite city (16:3), David's capture and Solomon's fame (16:13–14), the alliances with Egypt (16:26), Assyria (16:28; 2 Kings 16:7–10) and Chaldea (16:29), and child sacrifice (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6). By its place between the dated visions of 8:1 (592 BC) and 20:1 (591 BC) it was spoken before the siege that began in 588 BC.
views.C: Zimmerli, in his Hermeneia commentary, finds later layers in the chapter (his divisions are in that commentary and are not repeated here); Greenberg and Block read the chapter as a unity. Critics also ask how the chapter relates to Hosea 1–3, Jeremiah 2–3 and Ezekiel 23, and whether the marriage image does harm to women who hear it (see the section on the debate below).
views.J: The rabbis valued the chapter but did not want it read aloud as a prophetic reading: Rabbi Eliezer said 16:2 was not to be read as a haftarah (Mishnah Megillah 4:10; Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 25b). Rashi explains the birth customs of 16:4. The Passover Haggadah quotes 16:6–7 in its account of Israel's growth in Egypt.
views.X: Christians read the chapter as grace given to an unworthy people, as in Romans 5:6–8, and take its marriage language into the New Testament picture of the church as Christ's bride (Ephesians 5:25–27; Revelation 21:2). The Sodom verses (16:49–50) are set beside Matthew 10:15 and Jude 7.
views.F: Readers who expect a future restoration of Israel take 16:53–63 (the restored fortunes of Jerusalem and her sisters, and the everlasting covenant) as still to come. Others see it fulfilled in the church; Jewish hope reads it in the days of the Messiah.

deep.h: Which witnesses were read for chapters 16 to 19
deep.b: The Hebrew base for chapters 16 to 19 is the Leningrad Codex, read word by word with its Ketiv/Qere notes. The only Dead Sea scroll that preserves any verse of these chapters is 3QEzek (3Q1), which has parts of 16:31 to 33, read in the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription. For the Septuagint the witness is Codex Vaticanus as printed in Swete's edition; every such reading in the notes and variants is named by that codex, because Ziegler's critical edition and Papyrus 967 were not consulted for this part. Rashi, the Targum and Radak were read on Sefaria: Rashi on 16:4, 17:22 and chapter 19, the Targum on 17:22 to 23 and chapter 19, and Radak on 17:22. The Talmud passages cited (Makkot 24a and Berakhot 7a) were also read on Sefaria, in English. The Syriac, the Vulgate and other Hebrew manuscripts are named only where a commentary is given as the source.

deep.h: The harshest chapter: how to read it
deep.b:
Ezekiel 16 (and its twin in chapter 23) uses Israel's unfaithfulness the way Hosea 1–3 and Jeremiah 2–3 do, but at greater length and with plain sexual words. The Plain keeps the Hebrew's frankness and does not add to it (16:25, 26).

Two ways of reading it are old and a third is recent. The older readings take the story as a shock meant for men: the exiles who came to Ezekiel's house (8:1; 14:1; 20:1) were proud of Jerusalem, and the prophet turns her into a woman they must watch being shamed. Greenberg and Block defend it in this way. The woman is a city, the 'husband' is the LORD, and nothing in the chapter is a rule for how a man should treat his wife. The recent criticism asks what the image does to its readers. T. Drorah Setel (on Hosea), Renita Weems (Battered Love), Katheryn Darr and Julie Galambush argue that the image makes the husband's violence look like love, leaves him unjudged, and is easy to turn against women. Galambush notes that the 'wife' is also the city itself. Joyce surveys both sides.

The Plain does not decide. A reader can see that the chapter's last word is not the punishment but the covenant (16:60–63), and that the husband's own record is told as faithful: he gives life, clothes, jewels and an oath.

Ezekiel is the Bible's clearest statement of what Sodom's guilt was in the eyes of a prophet: pride, a full belly, quiet comfort, and no help for the poor and needy, followed by 'something abhorrent'. Jerusalem is worse than Sodom and Samaria because she had more (16:47–52). The restoration promised to both cities (16:53, 55) is the surprise of the chapter. See the notes at 16:49, 16:50 and 16:53 for the readings.

echoes: Hosea 1:2–3:5; Jeremiah 2:2; Jeremiah 3:1–5; Ezekiel 23; Isaiah 54:5; Ruth 3:9; Genesis 19:4–9; Isaiah 1:10; Matthew 10:15; Jude 7; Ephesians 5:25–32; Romans 5:6–8; Revelation 21:2

settings.what: The foundling bride and her faithlessness
settings.to: Jerusalem, addressed as a woman; heard by the exiles who came to Ezekiel's house in Babylon
settings.when: Undated; between the visions of 8:1 (592 BC) and 20:1 (591 BC), before the siege that began in 588 BC
settings.why: The exiles and the people still in Jerusalem trusted that the city's election made it safe. The speech retells the city's story as grace given to an unwanted child and answered by betrayal, so that the coming judgment is understood as just and not as the LORD's defeat.
settings.readers: The exiles who read the book after 586 BC, when the story explained why the city fell.
views: The traditional view is that Ezekiel spoke in Babylon about a city he could not see.
A minority view (Herntrich, Bertholet) put some of Ezekiel's work in Jerusalem itself.

settings.what: Like mother, like daughter: Samaria and Sodom
settings.when: The same time as the rest of the chapter
settings.why: Jerusalem measured herself against Samaria, which had fallen in 722 BC, and used Sodom as a curse (16:56). The speech shows that she is worse than both, and then promises the restoration of all three.
views: Greenberg and Block read this as part of one speech.
Some critics, Zimmerli among them, divide the chapter into layers; the divisions are in his commentary.

settings.to: Jerusalem, and through the book the exiles
settings.when: The same speech, or added after the fall (the views differ)
settings.why: The ending turns judgment into a promise: the LORD will remember the covenant of her youth and set up a lasting one, so that she is ashamed and silent when he forgives her.
settings.readers: The exiles after 586 BC read it as the answer to the question whether the LORD had finished with them.
views: Greenberg and Block hold that it belongs with the rest.
Some critics, Zimmerli among them, divide the chapter into layers; the divisions are in his commentary.

title: The Two Eagles and the Cedar Shoot
sum: Ezekiel is told to speak a riddle. A great eagle takes the top of a cedar in Lebanon and carries it to a city of traders. It plants a seed of the land beside plentiful water, and it becomes a low vine (17:1–6). A second eagle appears, and the vine turns its roots toward it (17:7–8). Will it prosper? (17:9–10).

The LORD explains the riddle at once. The first eagle is the king of Babylon, who took Jehoiachin and made Zedekiah king under a covenant. Zedekiah broke the oath by sending to Egypt for horses (17:11–18). He will die in Babylon, caught in the LORD's net (17:19–21). The chapter ends on a different note: the LORD himself will take a tender shoot from the top of the cedar and plant it on Israel's high mountain, where it will grow into a great cedar that shelters every bird (17:22–24).
readings: Read as politics

The riddle is a coded account of the years 597 to about 588 BC: the first deportation, Zedekiah's oath and his turn to Egypt. The vine is a vassal kingdom that was meant to stay low and loyal (17:14).
Read as a case about an oath
Ezekiel counts Zedekiah's oath as sworn to the LORD (17:19; 2 Chronicles 36:13). The sin is not a failure of statecraft but the breaking of a covenant.
Read as messianic hope
The Targum and Rashi hear in 17:22–24 a king from David's house; Radak names Zerubbabel; Christian readers see Christ. A plainer reading is that the LORD will re-plant the royal line after the exile.

views.H: The chapter fits 597 to 586 BC: Jehoiachin's deportation (2 Kings 24:12–15), Zedekiah enthroned under oath (2 Chronicles 36:13), his appeal to Egypt (Jeremiah 37:5–11) and his capture (2 Kings 25:4–7). The date of the oracle is debated: about 591 BC by its place, or later, nearer the revolt.
views.C: Greenberg and Block read the riddle, its explanation and the promise as one piece. Zimmerli, in his Hermeneia commentary, finds later layers in the chapter (his divisions are in that commentary and are not repeated here). The explanation in 17:11–21 is a prose commentary on the riddle, which is unusual and shows how much the exiles needed it spelled out.
views.J: The Targum of Jonathan reads the tender shoot as one 'from the sons of his sons' of David's house who will become 'a mighty king'; Rashi says 'the King Messiah'; Radak, in Hebrew, identifies the shoot with Zerubbabel, grandson of Jehoiachin (Sefaria texts).
views.X: Christians connect the tender shoot to Christ, the 'Branch' of Isaiah 11:1 and Jeremiah 23:5, and the birds under the tree to Jesus' mustard seed (Mark 4:30–32). Matthew traces Jesus through Jehoiachin (Matthew 1:11–12), which makes the shoot from Jehoiachin's line a natural link for some readers.
views.F: Readers who expect a future kingdom of David's son at Christ's return take 17:22–24 as still to come; Jewish hope looks for the Messiah of David's house.

deep.h: Why the LORD cares about an oath to Babylon
deep.b:
Ezekiel 17:19 calls the broken treaty 'my oath' and 'my covenant', because 2 Chronicles 36:13 says Nebuchadnezzar made Zedekiah swear by God. A treaty in the ancient Near East was sworn before the gods of both sides, so a vassal who broke it was a perjurer. Jeremiah gives the same counsel: submit (Jeremiah 27:12–15). The case of Gibeon, where Israel kept an oath it had been tricked into, shows the same seriousness (Joshua 9:19–20; 2 Samuel 21:1–2).

This is uncomfortable for a reader who sees Babylon as an oppressor. Ezekiel does not praise Babylon. He treats the eagle as the instrument of the LORD's judgment and Zedekiah as a man who tried to be free of a God-witnessed promise by trusting in horses (17:15). Commentators differ on how far this teaches submission to any empire; it teaches at least that vows should not be broken for convenience.

echoes: 2 Kings 24:8–20; 2 Chronicles 36:11–14; Jeremiah 27:1–15; Jeremiah 37:5–11; Ezekiel 12:13; Ezekiel 31:3–14; Isaiah 11:1; Mark 4:30–32; Daniel 4:10–12; Luke 1:52

settings.what: The riddle of the two eagles and the vine
settings.to: The house of Israel, the exiles who came to hear Ezekiel in Babylon
settings.when: Between the dated visions of 592 BC and 591 BC by the book's order; some date it nearer the revolt of Zedekiah
settings.why: The riddle makes the exiles see their own politics from outside. They are asked whether a vine that turns from its first planter to another will thrive.
views: About 591 BC, during the intrigues around a visit of Pharaoh Psammetichus II to Palestine (reported by commentaries).
About 589 to 588 BC, close to the revolt, when Hophra was king.

settings.what: The riddle explained: Zedekiah's broken oath
settings.to: The rebellious house, that is the exiles, speaking of Zedekiah in Jerusalem
settings.why: To show the exiles that the revolt their kinsmen at home were planning would fail, and that it was a breach of a promise made in the LORD's name.
settings.readers: After 586 BC the exiles read it as the account of why the last king fell.

settings.what: The tender shoot on the high mountain
settings.when: As above, or added after 586 BC (the views differ)
settings.why: The promise answers the fall of the cedar: the LORD himself will plant a new shoot, and the nations will see that he raises low things and brings down high ones.
settings.readers: Exiles and later readers in the Second Temple period took it as the promise of a Davidic king.
views: Greenberg and Block read the promise as part of the same chapter.
Some critics, Zimmerli among them, divide the chapter into layers; the divisions are in his commentary.

title: The Sour Grapes Proverb
sum: The exiles repeat a proverb: 'The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth go numb' (18:2). The LORD forbids it. All lives belong to him, the father's and the son's, and the person who sins is the one who will die (18:3–4). Then comes a teaching in three generations: a righteous man lives (18:5–9); his violent son dies (18:10–13); the grandson who sees his father's sins and does not copy them lives (18:14–18).

The people object that the son should bear the father's guilt (18:19) and that 'the Lord's way is not fair' (18:25, 29). The LORD answers that a wicked person who turns away from wrong will live, a righteous person who turns to wrong will die (18:21–28), and that it is their ways that are not fair. The chapter ends with a call: turn back, make a new heart and a new spirit, and live, because the LORD takes no pleasure in anyone's death (18:30–32).
readings: Read as an answer to fatalism

The exiles believed the sins of earlier kings, above all Manasseh's (2 Kings 21:10–15; 24:3–4), had already decided their fate. The proverb gave them an excuse not to change. Ezekiel replies that each generation stands before the LORD on its own record and that the door of repentance is open.
Read as a casebook of rulings

The three generations are set out like cases in a law book, each ending with a verdict, 'he will surely live' or 'he will surely die'. The list of the righteous man's deeds (18:5–9) resembles the entrance questions of Psalm 15 and Psalm 24.
Read as a teaching on sin and grace

Christian readers have used the chapter in the debate between Pelagius and Augustine, and on whether people inherit Adam's guilt (Romans 5:12–19), whether a righteous person can fall, and whether God wants all to be saved. See the cards on this page.

views.H: The proverb is quoted 'about the land of Israel' (18:2) and fits the exiles' belief that they paid for Manasseh (2 Kings 24:3–4). The chapter is undated, and its place between the visions of 592 and 591 BC dates it to about then.
views.C: The older critical view, from Wellhausen's time, held that Ezekiel 'invented' individual responsibility. Greenberg and Kaminsky answer that the older law and wisdom already knew it, and that Ezekiel is answering a fatalism. How the chapter relates to Jeremiah 31:29–30, which quotes the same saying as a thing of the past, is debated: both may quote a common proverb.
views.J: The Talmud reads Ezekiel as answering Moses: Makkot 24a has Moses say that the LORD visits the fathers' transgression on the sons (Exodus 34:7) and Ezekiel come and revoke it. Berakhot 7a fits the verses together by dividing children who adopt their ancestors' actions from children who do not, and cites Exodus 20:5 ('those who hate me') in the answer; that passage does not mention Ezekiel. Both were read on Sefaria in English.
views.X: Paul says God will repay each person according to his works (Romans 2:6) and that death came through one man (Romans 5:12–19). Churches differ on how these fit Ezekiel 18; see the cards. 18:23 and 18:32 are linked to 1 Timothy 2:4 and 2 Peter 3:9.
views.F: Futurist readers see the command to make a new heart (18:31) met by the promise to give one (36:26–27) in the future restoration of Israel; the chapter itself looks to the present of the exiles.

deep.h: Sour grapes, Moses and Jeremiah: how the texts fit
deep.b:
Exodus 20:5 says the LORD brings 'the fathers' guilt home to the children' (Exodus 20:5), Deuteronomy 24:16 says that in court 'children must not be put to death because of their fathers' (Deuteronomy 24:16), and 2 Kings 14:6 applies the rule to King Amaziah. Lamentations 5:7 says, 'we are the ones who carry their guilt' (Lamentations 5:7). Ezekiel 18 and Jeremiah 31:29–30 stand at the end of that conversation.

Readers have fit them in four main ways. One: Exodus 20:5 speaks of consequences that fall on families (a father's exile or ruin), while Deuteronomy 24:16 and Ezekiel speak of guilt and punishment before God, which are personal. Two: Exodus 20:5 says 'of those who hate me', which Berakhot 7a connects to children who adopt their ancestors' actions (that passage does not mention Ezekiel). Three: Ezekiel corrects an exiles' misuse of the saying and does not cancel Moses. Four: Ezekiel brings to the surface a principle already in the law (Kaminsky; Greenberg). Notice also that Ezekiel does not say that no one ever suffers for another's sin: the exiles were suffering for Manasseh's, and the chapter does not deny it. It says that they are not condemned for it if they turn.
deep.refs: Exodus 20:5; Exodus 34:7; Deuteronomy 24:16; 2 Kings 14:6; Lamentations 5:7; Jeremiah 31:29–30; 2 Kings 24:3–4; Ezekiel 18:20

deep.b: In the chapter 'live' is the opposite of 'die' in the coming judgment, not at first a word for the age to come. The offer is to the exiles: turn, and you will survive and be restored (compare 33:10–20). Later Jewish and Christian readers also heard eternal life in it; the verse does not make that its point. The Plain says 'live' and 'die' and leaves the meaning to the reader's tradition (see the note at 18:9).

echoes: Jeremiah 31:29–30; Lamentations 5:7; Exodus 20:5; Exodus 34:7; Deuteronomy 24:16; 2 Kings 14:6; Psalm 15; Psalm 24:3–6; Leviticus 18:19; Deuteronomy 23:19; Genesis 18:25; Ezekiel 11:19; Ezekiel 33:11; Ezekiel 36:26; Romans 2:6; Romans 5:12–19; 1 Timothy 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9

settings.what: The sour grapes proverb and the call to turn back
settings.to: The house of Israel: the exiles who used the proverb, and those at home who used it too ('about the land of Israel', 18:2)
settings.when: Undated; by the book's order about 592 to 591 BC, some years after the first deportation
settings.why: The exiles said they were being punished for their fathers' sins and so could do nothing. The speech forbids the saying, shows that each person is answerable, and calls them to turn so that they live.
settings.readers: The generation after 586 BC read it as the reason the door was still open after the fall.
views: The proverb is read as the exiles' cry that they suffer unfairly for earlier generations.
It is read as a way of avoiding responsibility; Ezekiel's answer, 'it is your ways', fits that.

traditions.q: Does 'a son will not bear the guilt of his father' (18:20) settle whether people inherit Adam's sin?
views: Original sin is 'contracted' and not 'committed', a state and not a personal act, passed on by propagation and removed in baptism (Council of Trent, session 5; Catechism 404 and 1263). Neither text cites Ezekiel 18.

The Confession of Dositheus (Jerusalem, 1672), Decree 6, says the first man fell in Paradise and that hereditary sin flowed to his descendants; it does not cite Ezekiel 18. John Romanides, in The Ancestral Sin, argued that the Orthodox tradition speaks of an inherited death and corruption and not of inherited guilt. He is one Orthodox teacher, and not every Orthodox writer puts it as he does.

Since the fall all people are born in sin, and this inborn disease is truly sin, bringing condemnation on those who are not born again by baptism and the Spirit (Augsburg Confession, article 2). The article does not cite Ezekiel 18.

The guilt of Adam's first sin was counted to all his descendants, and the same death in sin and corrupted nature passed on to them (Westminster Confession 6.3). The confession does not cite Ezekiel 18.
Original sin is the corruption of every person's nature, which only grace heals. Wesley defended the doctrine against those who denied it.

Adam's descendants inherit a nature inclined toward sin and become transgressors under condemnation once they are able to act morally (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 3). The article does not cite Ezekiel 18.

traditions.q: Can a righteous person lose life by turning away (18:24, 26)?
views: True believers can fall into grievous sins for a time but cannot fall away totally or finally (Westminster Confession 17; Canons of Dort, head 5). Neither text discusses Ezekiel 18:24. One way to fit the verse, which some propose, is to take the 'righteous' who die as righteous only in outward conduct; that is a reading of the passage and not a statement of either document.
All true believers endure to the end and will not fall from grace (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 5).
A person can lose sanctifying grace by mortal sin and be restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance (Catechism 1855–1861, 1446).

The Confession of Dositheus (1672), Decree 3, says God's grace co-operates with us and makes us persevere in the love of God, and that those who will not obey and co-operate with grace are condemned; Decree 14 says a person keeps the power to will or not to will to co-operate with grace. Neither decree cites Ezekiel 18.
A believer can fall from grace and be lost; Wesley argued this against the doctrine of final perseverance.
A believer can fall from faith by willful sin and be restored by repentance (Augsburg Confession, article 12); the elect are kept by God (Formula of Concord, article 11).

traditions.q: Does God want every person to be saved (18:23, 32)?
views: God's election is unconditional, and the gospel call is made sincerely to all who hear (Canons of Dort, heads 1 and 3/4). Calvin discusses Ezekiel 18:23 in the Institutes (book 3, chapter 24).
God wills that all be saved, and election is only to salvation: no one is chosen for damnation (Formula of Concord, article 11).
God's grace is free for all, not only for some elect; Wesley's sermon Free Grace argues against unconditional election on that ground.
God predestines no one to hell, and the Church prays that no one be lost (Catechism 1037, 1058).

The Confession of Dositheus (1672), Decree 3, says God predestined to glory those whom he chose and that those who will not obey and co-operate with grace are condemned. The decree does not cite Ezekiel 18.
Baptists are divided between Calvinist and non-Calvinist readings; the Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 5) calls election 'consistent with the free agency of man'.

title: A Lament for the Lions and the Vine
sum: Ezekiel is told to sing a lament for the leaders of Israel. The poem has two pictures. In the first, a lioness raises her cubs among lions. One cub learns to hunt people, is trapped by the nations and led away with hooks to Egypt (19:1–4). Her hope lost, she raises another, who also ravages the land. The nations trap him too and bring him in a cage to the king of Babylon, so that his roar is never heard on Israel's mountains again (19:5–9).

In the second picture the mother is a vine planted by water, with strong branches fit to be rulers' scepters. She is torn up in rage, scorched by the east wind and burned, and now stands in a dry desert (19:10–14). No king is named, and the LORD does not speak. The poem ends by calling itself a lament that has become one.
readings: Read as a funeral song for the dynasty
The lament mourns the line of David before it ends. The two cubs are kings taken away, one to Egypt in 609 BC and one to Babylon; the vine is the dynasty itself, uprooted in 586 BC.
Read beside chapters 15 and 17
The vine of 19:10–14 belongs with the useless vine of chapter 15 and the low vine of chapter 17. In chapter 17 the vine is the kingdom; here the 'mother' is the vine.

views.H: The first cub is usually Jehoahaz, taken to Egypt by Neco in 609 BC (2 Kings 23:31–34). The second is Jehoiachin (taken to Babylon in 597 BC; 2 Kings 24:8–15) or Zedekiah (2 Kings 25:6–7); Jehoiakim has also been proposed. Babylonian ration tablets list Jehoiachin as 'Ya'ukin, king of Judah'.
views.C: The poem is in the rhythm of the funeral lament and is among Ezekiel's best verse. Critics ask whether it was composed before 586 BC (as the visions place it, about 592 to 591) or after the fall, since it speaks of the vine's burning in the past tense; Codex Vaticanus reads a singular ruler and several lines of 19:7 and 19:10 differently (see the variants). Its two images recur in chapters 15, 17 and 31.
views.J: Rashi (Judaica Press translation, on Sefaria) takes the lament to be about the sons of Josiah: the first cub is Jehoahaz and the second Jehoiakim, and the mother is 'the congregation of Israel'. The Targum (on Sefaria) also reads the lioness and the vine as the Congregation of Israel and the cubs as kings, and its vine of 19:10 is Israel 'when performing the Torah'. The background is Jacob's blessing of Judah as a lion's cub (Genesis 49:9); the lion is Judah's emblem.
views.X: Christian readers set these failed lions against the Lion of the tribe of Judah in Revelation 5:5, and the vine against the promised shoot of 17:22–24. The chapter has no direct New Testament quotation.
views.F: There is no separate futurist reading of the chapter. The hope it lacks is supplied elsewhere: the new shoot (17:22–24) and the shepherd David (34:23–24; 37:24–25).

deep.b:
Ezekiel mixes images freely: Judah's kings are lion cubs (19:2–9), then branches (19:11), and the mother is a lioness (19:2) and a vine (19:10). The Hebrew has trouble in two places, 19:7 (what 'knew widows' means) and 19:10 ('in your blood'), and the variants say what Codex Vaticanus does. These hard places do not change the poem's main message, which is the loss of the royal line.

The lament avoids any statement of guilt. In chapter 17 Zedekiah is condemned for breaking an oath, but here the kings are mourned as captured animals and a burned vine. This restraint is part of the genre: a lament pities first. Another prophet's picture of a vine that fails is Isaiah 5:1–7.

echoes: Genesis 49:9–10; 2 Kings 23:31–34; 2 Kings 24:8–15; 2 Kings 25:6–7; Ezekiel 12:13; Ezekiel 17:5–10; Ezekiel 26:17; Ezekiel 32:2; Psalm 80:8–16; Revelation 5:5

settings.what: A lament for the leaders of Israel: the lioness and the vine
settings.by: The LORD commands it; Ezekiel sings it
settings.to: The exiles who gathered at Ezekiel's house, and the leaders and kings it mourns
settings.when: Undated; placed among the visions of 592 to 591 BC. That date fits if the second cub is Jehoiachin (taken in 597 BC) or Jehoiakim. If the second cub is Zedekiah (taken in 586 BC), the poem cannot have been spoken then and must be dated after 586 BC.
settings.why: A funeral song for kings who are gone or about to go. It teaches the exiles to grieve for the dynasty they trusted and not to hope for its quick return.
settings.readers: After 586 BC the exiles read it as the lament for the end of the monarchy; its last line says that it has become that.
views: Spoken about 592 to 591 BC, mourning the kings already taken and the kingdom's coming end.
Some critics think the last stanza (19:10–14) was shaped after 586 BC.
